questions.question: In a Fiat–Shamir-style signature, the verifier’s challenge is derived by hashing which data?
options: Only the message
Only the public key
The message (or message representative) concatenated with the signer’s commitment
Only the signer’s response
questions.explanation: Fiat–Shamir replaces an interactive challenge with a hash of the message (or its representative) and the commitment so both parties derive the same challenge.

questions.question: In ML-DSA/Dilithium, what is the purpose of the hint bits in the signature?
options: They increase the polynomial modulus q
They help the verifier reconstruct the same high bits that the signer hashed despite missing low-bit information
They let the signer skip hashing the message
They replace the need for a public key
questions.explanation: Hints guide rounding: the verifier can recover the same high-bit view (w1) the signer used, even though the verifier only computes an approximation.

questions.question: Dilithium/ML-DSA does arithmetic in which polynomial ring (conceptually)?
options: Z[x] / (x^n + q)
questions.explanation: Dilithium uses the negacyclic ring R_q = Z_q[x]/(x^n + 1), which enables fast NTT-based multiplication in real implementations.

questions.question: Why does verification compute something like A·z − c·t (or an approximation of it)?
options: To recover the random mask y exactly
To cancel the secret term involving s1 and relate the signature back to the commitment
To compute the public key from the signature
To avoid using any hash function
questions.explanation: With z = y + c·s1 and t = A·s1 + s2, the expression A·z − c·t simplifies to A·y − c·s2, linking verification back to the commitment without knowing s1.

questions.question: What does the signing-time rejection condition “HighBits(w − c·s2) must match HighBits(w)” ensure?
options: That the public key was generated correctly
That the verifier will hash the same w1 the signer hashed (so the challenge recomputes consistently)
That the signature is smaller than a threshold in bytes
That q is prime
questions.explanation: The verifier effectively sees a noised version of the commitment. The signer must ensure this noise does not change the high-bit view used for hashing, or verification would fail.

questions.question: Attack-themed: if an implementation removed the rejection sampling and always released z = y + c·s1, what becomes feasible from many signatures?
options: Recover the secret s1 by averaging z values across signatures
Factor the modulus q
Recover the hash function’s internal state exactly
Derive the verifier’s public key from the signature
questions.explanation: Without the abort/rejection logic, z retains a statistical dependence on s1; over many signatures, simple averaging attacks can reveal the secret.

questions.question: Why does ML-DSA split t into t1 and t0 (keeping only t1 in the public key)?
options: To increase signing speed by skipping matrix multiplication
To reduce public key size by dropping low bits (t0), while still letting the signer correct rounding using t0
To avoid using an extendable-output function (XOF)
To make signatures deterministic
questions.explanation: t0 contains low bits that are not published to save space; the signer retains t0 and provides hints so the verifier can still derive the correct high-bit view.

questions.question: Which encoding/decoding practice is most important to prevent malleability and cross-implementation bugs?
options: Allow multiple different byte encodings to decode to the same signature
Use non-canonical encodings and normalize silently during verification
Require a single canonical encoding and reject out-of-range or non-canonical inputs
Skip all range checks for performance
questions.explanation: Cryptographic encodings must be canonical: verification should reject malformed or non-canonical inputs rather than “fixing them up”, to avoid malleability and interop issues.
